source: Macina, Kapur & Sachan (2026) The Assistance Dilemma: Learning to Teach via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (EDUARDO), arXiv 2610.06446
finding: Language models default to being maximal answerers. They over-scaffold and hand over solutions. The authors name this the assistance dilemma (too little help vs too much) and train tutors with reinforcement learning against a frozen student model.
numbers: Student: frozen Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Dialogs up to 22 turns. Tutors trained at 4B, 9B, 14B, 27B. Post-test uses 16 student samples on an unseen near-transfer variant (8,671 problem pairs from BigMath).
quote: LLMs ... default to being maximally capable answerers rather than teachers
limits: Student is a small LLM, not a human. Results come from simulation plus MathDial and Eedi next-turn scoring.
agent_relevance: A model that wants to help will give away too much. Our agent needs a hard rule on how much help it gives itself, not a hope that it holds back.

source: Macina, Kapur & Sachan (2026) The Assistance Dilemma: Learning to Teach via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (EDUARDO), arXiv 2610.06446 - ablation table 2
finding: If the reward is just the student's learning gain, telling the answer is not punished. Without the binary no-handover gate, the tutor handed over the solution in 61% of dialogs at about the same gain.
numbers: 4B leave-one-out: full recipe transfer gain +0.25, leak 31%; without gates +0.23, leak 61%; without masking +0.24, leak 13%; without near-transfer +0.23, leak 47%; base Qwen3.5-4B +0.10 transfer, leak 17%.
quote: a behavior that costs nothing is not unlearned
limits: Single scale (4B) for the ablation; leak is judged by an LLM judge. Gain barely moved between ablations (0.23 to 0.25), so gain alone did not separate teaching from telling.
agent_relevance: Measure help by what the learner can do alone afterwards (the masked post-test idea), and add a binary cost for handing over. For our agent: count results that survive when the helper's text is removed.

source: Macina, Kapur & Sachan (2026) The Assistance Dilemma: Learning to Teach via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (EDUARDO), arXiv 2610.06446 - behavior shifts (Fig 2b)
finding: RL on single-problem dialogs trained OUT support fading. The move 'ask for independent work' fell to 0.0%, because fading only pays across several problems, not inside one episode. Prompting for justification more than doubled.
numbers: Move H (independent work) to 0.0%. Move G (prompt for justification) 9.0% to 21.8%. Move A (guiding questions) 23.2% to 41.4%. Move C (explaining) 18.5% to 3.9%. Move F (supplying answers) 15.5% to 2.2%.
quote: support fading ... never pays before test within our single-problem dialog horizon
limits: Episode horizon is one problem. Authors say fading would need a multi-problem reward horizon. No test of fading on human learners.
agent_relevance: Direct machine evidence that fading needs a horizon longer than one problem. Our S0 fade-help-by-pass-rate rule must be scored across the class of tasks, not within one item.

source: Macina, Kapur & Sachan (2026) The Assistance Dilemma: Learning to Teach via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (EDUARDO), arXiv 2610.06446 - results vs base and frontier
finding: Post-trained EDUARDO-27B matches Gemini 3.1 Pro on MathTutorBench and the trained models beat their base models on pedagogy at every size, while keeping diagnostic accuracy.
numbers: Eduardo-4B vs base 4B on MathDial middle-turn: reward-model score 7.92 vs 2.08, win rate vs human teacher 78.0% vs 30.2%. Eedi: 8.83 vs 3.56, 72.4% vs 38.7%.
limits: Judge is Gemini-3.1-Pro; judge dependence is a risk. Not a human learning study.
agent_relevance: Restraint in helping is trainable but is not the default. A scaffold-only agent cannot train it, so the restraint has to live in code.

source: Gure et al. (2026) Structuring versus Problematizing: How LLM-based Agents Scaffold Learning in Diagnostic Reasoning (PharmaSim Switch), LAK26, arXiv 2604.09158
finding: A between-groups test of two LLM scaffold styles (structuring vs problematizing) found no interaction with prior knowledge. Scenario complexity mattered more than prior knowledge or scaffold style. This is a null for an expertise-reversal-type interaction.
numbers: N=63 pharmacy technician apprentices (31 structuring, 32 problematizing; 6 excluded). Multilevel models: no effect of strategy pretest or conceptual-knowledge pretest, of group, or of group-by-scenario interaction. Scenario effect p < .05 for the interpersonal-relationship and possible-causes strategies.
limits: Small N, vocational students with fairly uniform prior knowledge, two scaffold types rather than scaffold vs none. A small interaction cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: An LLM scaffold style did not visibly flip with learner level here. Do not assume the reversal shows up in every LLM tutor study.

source: Gure et al. (2026) Structuring versus Problematizing: How LLM-based Agents Scaffold Learning in Diagnostic Reasoning (PharmaSim Switch), LAK26, arXiv 2604.09158 - how the mentor behaved
finding: The LLM mentor matched scaffold type to the strategy being practiced: near-pure structuring for the checklist strategy, a near-even mix for possible-causes. Structuring gave more accurate active and interactive turns; problematizing gave more constructive turns.
numbers: Possible-causes strategy in the structuring-heavy arm: structuring about 51.8% of mentor moves. Problematizing-heavy arm: problematizing 88.3% (possible causes) and 75% (interpersonal), 47.3% for checklist.
limits: Percentages come from rubric coding of the mentor, not from learner outcomes.
agent_relevance: Procedural parts of a task take structure; generative parts take open prompts. Our schema could key help type to the operator, not only the amount.

source: Nazaretsky (2026) Tailoring Scaffolding to Diagnostic Strategies: Theory-Informed LLM-Based Agents, LAK26 workshop, arXiv 2605.04996
finding: A proposal, not a result: a hybrid LLM mentor that switches scaffold type by what knowledge the strategy needs (Knowledge-Learning-Instruction framework). A study with 173 apprentices ran in January 2026; results not yet reported.
numbers: N=173 collected. No outcome numbers in the paper.
limits: No data. Use only as a pointer to a pending study.
agent_relevance: Watch for the result; it is the nearest LLM test of matching support to learner state in a field setting.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks, arXiv 2602.12670 (v4)
finding: Curated procedural help (Skills) raised agent pass rates in all 18 model-harness setups, but the size of the lift varied widely. The strongest systems were not the biggest winners.
numbers: 87 tasks, 8 domains, 3 trials. No-Skills 33.9% to curated 50.5% (+16.6 pp; 25.5% normalized). Range +4.1 to +25.7 pp. Largest lifts: OpenHands+GLM 5.1 +25.7, Gemini CLI+Gemini 3.1 Pro +24.8, OpenHands+DeepSeek V4 Pro +23.2.
quote: Skill efficacy is therefore an empirical property of a specific agent stack rather than a universal constant.
limits: Harnesses differ, so lift is not a clean ability effect; no human-style expertise split. Tasks have verifiers.
agent_relevance: Closest agent-world analogue of help depending on who gets it. It supports adapting help by a measured pass rate.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks, arXiv 2602.12670 (v4) - high baseline case
finding: A model with a strong baseline gained little from help: high base capability did not imply high Skill leverage. The authors say gains are smaller or negative when models already have strong priors or the Skill adds overhead.
numbers: OpenHands + Gemini 3.5 Flash: no-Skills baseline 41.1%, gain only +7.1 pp. 13 of 87 tasks had negative Skill deltas; largest -7.4 pp (exam-block-sequencing, suricata-custom-exfil).
quote: smaller or negative when models already have strong priors or the Skill adds overhead
limits: One configuration plus an authors' interpretation. Not a controlled expertise manipulation.
agent_relevance: The expertise-reversal pattern in machines in its weak form: help adds less when the model already knows. A clean test would give the same help at several baselines.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks, arXiv 2602.12670 (v4) - self-generated help
finding: Help the agent writes for itself hurt. Self-generated Skills fell below the no-Skills baseline on all three dedicated harnesses, while curated Skills added +18.2 to +24.8 pp on the same setups.
numbers: Self-generated minus no Skills: -8.1 pp (Claude Code + Opus 4.7; 43.0 to 34.9), -11.3 pp (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 pp (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro).
limits: Self-written help came from one skill-creator route; trajectories audited by the authors.
agent_relevance: Do not let the agent write its own scaffold on the fly and trust it. External, checked help only (fits G2, G3).

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks, arXiv 2602.12670 (v4) - how much help
finding: More help text was not better. Compact focused guidance beat exhaustive documentation. Too many Skills per task also lowered the gain.
numbers: 1 Skill +18.0 pp; 2-3 Skills +19.0 pp; 4+ Skills +10.1 pp. By length (summary text): compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7 pp.
quote: focused procedural guidance beats exhaustive prose
limits: Observational split of tasks by skill length, not a randomized dose. The summary and the table label two buckets slightly differently.
agent_relevance: A dose-response curve for guidance in agents: a little helps, a lot erases the benefit. Keep any help block short.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks, arXiv 2602.12670 (v4) - small model plus help
finding: Help can stand in for model size: a smaller model with Skills beat stronger models without them.
numbers: MiniMax M2.7 with Skills 34.9% exceeded OpenHands+GLM 5.1 no-Skills 32.7% and OpenHands+MiniMax M3 no-Skills 29.7%.
limits: Cross-harness comparisons mix model and harness effects.
agent_relevance: Help matters most for weaker setups, the novice side of the reversal. The schema's gain should be largest on the weakest model.

source: Teach to Learn: Hint Annealing for Self-improving LLM Reasoning (HATCH), Tencent Yuanbao / HKUST, arXiv 2609.34975
finding: Training with hints on failed problems can teach the model to solve WITH hints, not without. The authors call it hinted reward shift. More hinted trajectories speed early learning but hurt later; the fix is to anneal (fade) the hint weight online.
numbers: Figure 2c: multiple hints per failed query give faster early gains, then decline; a single hint keeps improving more slowly.
quote: hinted trajectories should contribute most when many queries lack learning signal and recede as that signal emerges
limits: Training-time hints in RL, not a prompt. Small models (1B to 8B).
agent_relevance: Machine version of the fading rule: hints help most when many tries fail and should recede as the model gets signal alone. Supports fade as pass rate rises.

source: Teach to Learn: Hint Annealing for Self-improving LLM Reasoning (HATCH), Tencent Yuanbao / HKUST, arXiv 2609.34975 - no-hint accuracy, table 1
finding: Annealed hints beat plain GRPO and two other hint or curriculum methods on no-hint test accuracy, and the gain was larger for the larger model.
numbers: Average no-hint accuracy: Llama-3.2-1B 4.49 base, 6.07 GRPO, 7.09 QuestA; Qwen3-1.7B 32.24 base, 36.43 GRPO, 37.01 QuestA, 37.15 HiLL, 39.99 HATCH; Qwen3-8B 38.02 base, 47.58 GRPO, 49.07 QuestA, 49.44 HiLL, 53.76 HATCH. Abstract: +1.02, +2.84, +4.32 pp over best prior method.
limits: Math benchmarks only; one table, no seeds shown; QuestA was reimplemented by the authors.
agent_relevance: Fading beats keeping or dropping help in a trained system. Not a prompt-only result, so it supports the principle for our agent only.

source: Commey (2026) When Generic Prompt Improvements Hurt: Evaluation-Driven Iteration for LLM Applications, arXiv 2601.22025 (v2)
finding: Adding generic extra rules to a prompt is not monotonic. It helped strict extraction but hurt RAG citation compliance for one 7B model.
numbers: Llama 3 8B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct via Ollama, 30 cases per suite, 5 prompt conditions. Qwen 2.5 RAG: 26/30 (86.7%) baseline to 9/30 (30.0%) with generic rules appended to the user prompt. Qwen 2.5 instruction following: 20/30 baseline, 17/30 in one condition, 23/30 in another.
limits: Small local models, 30 cases per cell, wide intervals (26/30 has 70.3 to 94.7). Not a learner-expertise manipulation.
agent_relevance: Extra help can cut a task the model was already doing well. Every help element must be tested at equal tokens against the plain model (our G7).

source: Tang et al. (2025) The Few-shot Dilemma: Over-prompting Large Language Models, arXiv 2509.13196
finding: More in-context examples help up to a model-specific optimum, then performance falls. The turning point differs by model; the GPT models did not show a significant drop, while smaller open models (Llama, Gemma) declined sharply.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, DeepSeek-V3, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B; datasets PROMISE and PURE. Top weighted F1 about 90.6% (DeepSeek-V3) and 90.0% (Llama-3.1-8B) on the relabeled set.
limits: PDF text was partly garbled, so exact curve values were not read; only the main pattern and the top scores. One domain (requirements classification).
agent_relevance: The best amount of help differs by model, so tune it per model rather than fixing it.

source: Singh et al. (2026) Hint-Writing with Deferred AI Assistance: Fostering Critical Engagement in Data Science Education, arXiv 2604.19931
finding: Order of help mattered. Students who wrote a hint first and saw the AI hint afterwards (deferred) wrote the best hints. On-demand AI help came in between, and the no-AI baseline was lowest.
numbers: Randomized, N=97 graduate students, three conditions. Hint quality: deferred condition beta=1.096, SE=0.37, p=0.003; on-demand AI beta=0.75, SE=0.34, p=0.03. Another comparison: deferred vs baseline p=0.01, on-demand vs baseline p=0.08.
limits: Hint-writing task with graduate students; effects were significant in week 1 (p=0.02) but not in week 2.
agent_relevance: Try alone first, then get help, is fading in time. For our agent: attempt first, show help only after a failed check.

source: LearnLM Team, Google & Eedi (2025) AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: an exploratory RCT in UK classrooms, arXiv 2512.23633
finding: A pedagogy-tuned model under expert tutor supervision did at least as well as human tutors on every outcome. Interactive tutoring beat static hints for remediation.
numbers: N=165 students, five UK secondary schools. Tutors approved 76.4% of drafted messages with zero or minimal edits. Novel problems on later topics solved: 66.2% (LearnLM) vs 60.7% (human tutors), +5.5 pp.
limits: Exploratory RCT, every message supervised by a human, not autonomous. No analysis by prior attainment found in the text opened.
agent_relevance: Socratic, question-first support from a model can match experts when checked. It does not test expertise reversal.

source: Schmucker, Pachapurkar, Bala, Shah & Mitchell (2025) Learning to Optimize Feedback for One Million Students: multi-armed and contextual bandits, arXiv 2508.00270
finding: A deployed tutor learned which hint to give per question from data of one million students. Personalizing by student features gave little extra, because effect differences between students were usually small.
numbers: 43,000 assistance actions assessed offline; 166,000 practice sessions in the online check of the multi-armed-bandit policies. Some actions for some questions show effect heterogeneity, often too small for contextual bandits to beat a good one-for-all policy.
limits: Not an LLM; hints chosen from a fixed menu on one platform (CK-12). Features were ability estimates and response times.
agent_relevance: Tempers the effect: personalization by learner level may add little beyond a well-chosen default. Start with one tuned default and fade it; do not over-engineer personalization.

source: Thomas, Borchers, Bhushan, Gatz, Gupta & Koedinger (2025) LLM-Generated Feedback Supports Learning If Learners Choose to Use It, arXiv 2506.17006
finding: On-demand gpt-3.5-turbo feedback helped only some learners. Learners likely to use it scored higher at posttest anyway; after adjusting for that selection, two of seven lessons showed real benefit.
numbers: 885 tutor learners, over 2,600 lesson completions, 7 lessons. Standardized effect sizes 0.28 and 0.33 in the two lessons, after propensity adjustment.
limits: Observational with propensity scoring; only the abstract and introduction were read.
agent_relevance: Who asks for help is confounded with who needs it. An agent that triggers help from a check signal avoids this selection problem.

source: Prather et al. (2024) The Widening Gap: The Benefits and Harms of Generative AI for Novice Programmers, ICER 2024, arXiv 2405.17739
finding: Search-result summary only: in 21 lab sessions, novices with weak metacognition were hindered by generative AI, while others sped up by using it for code they already meant to write and ignoring bad suggestions.
numbers: 21 lab sessions (eye tracking, interviews). Not opened; from a search summary.
limits: Not opened this session. Qualitative, small sample.
agent_relevance: A human parallel to expertise reversal for AI help itself: the same tool helps those who know and hurts those who do not. Treat as a lead.

source: Koedinger & Aleven (2007) Exploring the assistance dilemma in experiments with Cognitive Tutors, Educ Psychol Rev 19
finding: Named the assistance dilemma that the 2026 LLM tutor papers build on: when to give help and when to withhold it. Older computational tutors (Cognitive Tutors) are the line this belongs to.
numbers: Not opened. Only cited in arXiv 2610.06446 (opened).
limits: Not opened. Cited secondhand.
agent_relevance: Older computational line behind our fade rule.

source: Dinucu-Jianu, Macina, Daheim, Hakimi, Gurevych & Sachan (2025) From Problem-Solving to Teaching Problem-Solving (TutorRL)
finding: Earlier RL tutor trained against a simulated student. The EDUARDO paper says its reward re-tests the same problem with the tutor's words in context, so telling raises reward and a leakage penalty is needed.
numbers: Not opened. Description is from arXiv 2610.06446's related-work section.
limits: Not opened. The claim about this paper is as reported by the later paper.
agent_relevance: RL-trained help can reward the wrong thing; same logic as reward hacking in any self-grading agent.

source: Lee et al. (2026) EduClaw-Bench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Pedagogical LLM Agents with Simulated Learners, arXiv 2608.03206
finding: A 30-day simulated-learner benchmark found tutoring quality depends on model and harness together, and almost no combination sustained good tutoring over the whole horizon.
numbers: 10 agent adapters, 3 model tiers, 55 scenarios; learner calibration ECE 0.049 over 176,187 (run, day) pairs; one adapter's Help score collapsed 3.19 to 2.30, per-epoch 3.18, 2.50, 1.85, no recovery.
limits: Simulated learner built from knowledge tracing; does not test fading directly. Reading of 'sustain' is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Help quality decays across a long run. A fade rule has to be re-checked as the horizon grows, not set once.

source: Search note (2026-11-01) angle C coverage
finding: Searched OpenAlex, arXiv and the web for direct tests of expertise reversal in language models or LLM agent loops. No paper was found that gives the same help to models of different ability and reports a reversal. Closest are SkillsBench (smaller gain at a strong baseline) and hint annealing in RL.
numbers: Fewer than 8 web searches plus OpenAlex queries; the arXiv API returned HTTP 429 after the first batch.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search. evidence_b and evidence_d already hold Scaf-GRPO, QuestA, Meincke et al. and DeepSeek-R1 few-shot results, not repeated here.
agent_relevance: The reversal in machines is untested as a clean experiment. Our own bench could run it: the same help block at several plain-model pass rates.
